title: Testing, Testing, One Two, One Two
author: Claudia Lewis
summary: Claudia Lewis walks through how to respond when an end-of-topic test goes badly, splitting the response by whether the result was a surprise. If a teacher was blindsided, she argues that's itself diagnostic: it means checking-for-understanding, homework review, or circulating weren't producing accurate data, and she recommends auditing whether mini-whiteboards are used for whole-class data (versus only cold-calling individuals) and whether students can covertly copy answers during retrieval tasks, since both would produce false confidence in what students actually know. If the poor result wasn't a surprise, she pushes back on any implicit acceptance of underperformance, arguing those already-flagged students, often the same students eligible for pupil premium or with additional needs, should be seated for maximum visibility and prioritised in every checking-for-understanding pass, not written off as expected underachievers. Throughout, she recommends a phone call home in both scenarios, both to rule out non-academic causes and to build parental goodwill for whatever intervention follows. She closes with a footnote skeptical of end-of-unit assessments generally, arguing they're often no better than mocks at diagnosing whether a student didn't know content or was simply tripped up by question wording.
points: Lewis argues an unexpected poor test result is itself diagnostic evidence that a teacher's checking-for-understanding, homework review, or circulation isn't producing accurate real-time data.
She flags a specific failure mode: retrieval tasks where students can covertly copy answers or look things up, producing an illusion of knowledge that doesn't survive an actual assessment.

For students whose underperformance wasn't surprising, she explicitly rejects treating that as acceptable, arguing those students, often pupil-premium or SEN, should get seated for maximum visibility and prioritised checking, not written off.
She recommends a phone call home in both surprise and non-surprise scenarios, framing it as both a diagnostic tool (ruling out external causes) and a relationship-building move with parents.
quotes: An unexpected poor result means something has gone wrong somewhere. If you've been blindsided, it means your checking for understanding in class isn't getting you accurate data.
Are you going back to the board to reteach content if there’s a <80% success rate? If the answer to any of these questions is ‘no’, then that’s the first place to start.
When students are attempting retrieval tasks, do they have to use their memory, or are they allowed to look things up, thereby not actually engaging in retrieval?
Just because you’re not surprised that a student has done poorly, doesn’t mean it’s okay that they’ve done poorly.
These students should be the ones sat at the front, the ones you can watch like a hawk and come down on like a ton of bricks when they start slacking.
I think end of unit assessments are largely a waste of time, they're just as useless as mocks for identifying areas of weakness.
